item.title: Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders Condemn Tech ‘Oligarchs’ and Demand A.I. Reforms
item.description:
In thundering, back-to-back speeches, Senator Bernie Sanders and Stephen K. Bannon on Tuesday denounced the billionaires who run the country’s largest tech companies and urged Americans to demand tighter restrictions on artificial intelligence before its capabilities exceed human control.

The unusual public appearances by the country’s elder democratic socialist and a leading architect of the MAGA movement, at a conference in Washington, underscored the deep and rising anxiety over the potential destructive power of artificial intelligence. As calls to regulate the technology have grown louder, transcending political allegiances, there is little consensus from Congress or the White House about what a national policy would look like.

“When you are racing towards a cliff,” Mr. Sanders said, “you hit the brakes.” He added, “We are at a dangerous and unprecedented moment in world history. And it is imperative for all of us to stand up.”

Everyone attending the event, the Pro-Human Assembly, seemed in agreement about the threat that A.I. may someday wipe out humanity. But for a few hours, A.I. produced a less catastrophic outcome: It united the participants — Republican and Democratic politicians, evangelical Christian, Mormon and Catholic leaders, artists and others — in agreement that human beings, not machines, should control their own destinies.

The conference, which was hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute, drew several hundred people who listened to hours of speeches about the deepening anxiety in Silicon Valley, Washington and beyond about the race to rein in A.I. before its computing power becomes unstoppable.

A slogan embroidered on hats being handed out to attendees captured the sentiment shared by most carbon-based life-forms in the room: “Keep the future human.”

Such concerns have intensified with surprising speed lately.

Last week, an Anthropic researcher who had previously worked at OpenAI went public with his decision to resign, saying that he believed both companies were acting irresponsibly.

In response, the chief executives of the A.I. start-ups Anthropic and OpenAI acknowledged their own fears that their technologies are advancing at an alarming pace.

Seven in 10 Americans said they are afraid A.I. will weaken human bonds, according to a poll released this week by Elon University, and about six in 10 say A.I.’s potential to take over most human tasks will undermine an individual’s sense of purpose. A separate poll from The New York Times found that 61 percent of likely voters oppose the construction of data centers, the massive warehouses that power A.I.

But there is little agreement in Washington about how to mandate a slower, more regulated approach to A.I. development. The White House and congressional leaders have sent conflicting signals. On Monday, President Trump dismissed calls for safety guardrails on A.I., calling fears of the technology as a “hoax.” He warned he could take criminal action against the heads of A.I. companies for any harms created by their technologies.

Anthropic declined to comment and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and its partner, Microsoft, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. OpenAI and Microsoft have denied those claims.)

At the conference, speakers pitched a wide array of regulatory proposals, without consensus on whether regulators should intervene to fully stop the development of A.I. Some leaders conceded they struggled to understand the technology.

Representative Greg Casar, for instance, proposed one solution the tech industry has resisted. “The answer is simple: We ban A.I. systems that are too powerful for humans to control,” said Mr. Casar, Democrat of Texas.

The speeches on Tuesday also conveyed, with a sense of disbelief from the speakers, about how such obvious, uncontroversial statements about human dignity needed to be said out loud.

“I can’t believe I have to say this,” said Representative Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts. “The future we all want is human. It’s nonnegotiable.”

“If we lose grip on this technology, we don’t lose grip as Republicans or Democrats,” Ms. Trahan continued, as she was interrupted by applause. “We lose it as human beings.”

A Catholic archbishop, an evangelical pastor and an elder from the Mormon Church voiced a wide variety of concerns.

Salvatore J. Cordileone, the archbishop of San Francisco, urged people to seize their agency while they still can. “We have to be the masters of A.I.,” he said.

His speech raised an unknown that weighed heavily on the minds of many at the conference: Is it already too late?

This heavy question and others were left largely unanswered.

Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, asked whether humans would be living without purpose in a world of “frictionless existence,” where he said A.I. is expected to solve most problems.

Ashley Judd, the actor and the chief negotiator for the union SAG-AFTRA, spoke for many in Hollywood about how A.I. has led to the spread of images of sexual abuse and disinformation.

Parents of teenagers who died by suicide after developing relationships with chatbots delivered tearful appeals for child safety regulation.

Representative Chip Roy, Republican of Texas, recalled encounters with constituents who described feeling powerless as data centers went up in their communities, with little consultation, and as their children became obsessed with technology they didn’t understand.

Technology, he said, should be a tool that people consciously decide to use, not the other way around. “We are not supposed to be tools for data collection and technology,” he said.

Both Mr. Sanders and Mr. Bannon decried the absence of any meaningful input into A.I. regulation by the tens of millions of working Americans whose lives they said would be most upended by A.I.

Mr. Sanders has introduced legislation to pause development of data centers and called for Mr. Trump to form an accord with the president of China, Xi Jinping, to ban superintelligent A.I.

Mr. Bannon said he doesn’t believe legislation will slow down A.I. because of Congress’ inaction. Instead, he called for presidential executive order to slow down development and ensure the biggest tech firms aren’t able to extend their power through their grip on the A.I. industry.

“American citizens are not going to be supplicants to the oligarchs anymore,” declared Mr. Bannon, who noted that despite the obvious areas of disagreement between him and Mr. Sanders, the high stakes of the moment demanded partisanship be set aside.

“We have to rise above it,” Mr. Bannon said. “This is a hinge in history.”

item.title: Age Limits for Social Media Outlined by European Union
item.description:
The European Union outlined plans on Wednesday to restrict social media use for children under 15, an aggressive step to curtail access to apps like TikTok and Instagram across the 27-nation bloc.

The proposal, called the EU Kids Act, would bar children under the age of 13 from using social media, Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, the bloc’s executive branch, said in a speech in Strasbourg, France. Teens aged 13 and 14 could access new “mini accounts” supervised by parents that would limit their contact with strangers and overall screen time. Access to a more independent account would be allowed from age 15.

“It is not about our minors accessing social media. It is about when and how do we allow social media to access minors,” said Ms. von der Leyen during an annual State of the Union address.

The act would be one of the biggest policy steps to date in a global movement to limit children’s screen time and access to social media. The European Union, home to 450 million people, has long been an aggressive regulator of the tech industry, using its power to force companies to change products and policies. In recent years, Apple changed its App Store, Google its search engine and Meta its data-privacy practices to comply with European laws and regulations.

The European Union is trying to balance regulating the tech industry while encouraging the development of artificial intelligence and other technologies that could drive economic growth. On Wednesday, Ms. von der Leyen raised concerns about the safety risks of A.I., but said the region must expand development or risk falling behind the United States and China.

“We need to stay in the race,” she said.

Ms. von der Leyen has made child safety online a priority amid growing concern among parents, mental health experts and policymakers. In the European Union, young people now spend four to six hours per day on screens, she said.

“Children are pulled ever deeper into feeds designed to keep them scrolling,” she said.

Australia last year became the first country in the world to bar children under 16 from social media. Since then, countries including France, Denmark and Malaysia have carried out or are considering similar rules.

In the United States, Meta last month agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion in penalties and to make major changes to its products as part of a landmark legal settlement over claims the addictive design of its products engaged children. The company, which owns Instagram and Facebook, said it would limit how long teenagers can spend on its platforms and limit features like infinite scroll.

The European Commission is expected to release full details of the social media rules on Thursday. The proposal will then wind its way through the E.U. lawmaking process, which requires agreement from member countries and the 720-member European Parliament.

One central question will be how to enforce the rules. In Australia, critics have said that teenagers are easily sidestepping the blocks and that the law has not fulfilled its promise.

Policymakers have explored the introduction of age verification technology that has raised concerns among privacy advocates.

“Children clearly need better protection online, but age verification is not a silver bullet and would raise serious privacy and data protection concerns of its own,” Agustín Reyna, director of the European consumer watchdog BEUC, said in a statement this week.

item.title: How Do You Share 175 Years of New York Times History?
item.description:
Times Insider explains who we are and what we do, and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how our journalism comes together.

One hundred and seventy-five years is a long time. The telephone is only 150 years old. Air-conditioning didn’t come on the scene until 124 years ago. TV is practically a baby at just 100.

So with The New York Times celebrating its 175th anniversary this fall — the first issue was published on Sept. 18, 1851 — you might think that David Shipley, the editor overseeing coverage of the milestone, would have been daunted trying to get his hands around it.

On the contrary, he was excited by the challenge.

“It’s been such a joy wandering back 175 years through the news canon, just having an opportunity to see the world as it’s been reflected in this remarkable institution,” he said.

From this week through mid-December, dozens of writers will contribute nearly 50 stories exploring The Times’s triumphs and shortcomings. A special issue of The New York Times Magazine is planned, as is a commemorative section of the paper. All of the work will be free to read online.

In an interview, Mr. Shipley reflected on the challenge of representing the breadth of The Times’s history and what he hopes readers will take away from the project. These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

What’s the value of looking back and taking stock?

It’s been a giant lesson in perspective. You see context and precedent where you didn’t necessarily see it before. You see that challenges we face today are challenges we’ve faced along the way, in just about every realm. Maybe most of all, when you look back, you come away with deep admiration for the stubborn persistence of our values and commitment.

What are you most excited about?

Unfair question. I’m excited by all of it. But we have a weekly series we’re calling Eyewitness that tells the stories of what some of our journalists have seen and captured. Dan Barry is writing about Samuel Wilkeson, one of two correspondents The Times sent to Gettysburg. He found his fallen son on the battlefield and wrote a front-page article that’s both a remembrance of those who died in the war and an account of the battle.

We also have first-person pieces from some special reporters, including one by John Darnton, the former Warsaw bureau chief, who’s writing about his experience in Poland when martial law was imposed in 1981. And there are reflections by Nick Kristof, our former Beijing bureau chief, about witnessing the Tiananmen Square protests in China in 1989, and Isabel Wilkerson about covering the floods in the Midwest in 1993. It felt important to emphasize the humanness of the report — that we aren’t algorithms; we aren’t A.I.; we are humans out there observing these events.

And we’ll have a series of stand-alone projects: one set of mini-essays on objects associated with our work and another on first mentions — the first time a person, place or thing appeared in the paper. We have writers like Lena Dunham and Margaret Atwood reflecting on the front pages from the day they were born; and a package in which current Times culture critics interact with the work of their predecessors. There’s lots more, too.

How did you make sure you were representing the entirety of Times coverage?

This was never going to be encyclopedic. The hope is that, between the pieces produced by the various groups — Opinion, the Magazine, the news coverage — you will get a sense of comprehensiveness. But gaps are inevitable. And we are definitely doing this with humility.

How did you think about spotlighting roles of people behind the scenes like editors, page designers and researchers?

We wanted this to be much more about sharing with readers the events that have been recorded, rather than the us of it. There are so many amazing stories to tell about the people here who make this thing every day, but this was not, in the end, where we landed. The bigger point was to say, “Hey, let’s remind you of the world that’s been captured, so you can both learn about history but also put your own life in context.”

How are we wrestling with uncomfortable parts of our history, such as the Jayson Blair fabrication and plagiarism scandal or the shortcomings in our reporting on Saddam Hussein’s weapons program in the run-up to the Iraq war?

I was glad to have Adam Nagourney write a piece on how The Times has handled corrections because I admire his book about the paper’s recent history. As Adam points out, the modern era is the one in which The Times made huge changes in the way it scrutinized itself and responded to criticism. We chose to focus on the moments that figured largest.

The ways we’ve addressed our mistakes and blind spots are in some ways our proudest moments, especially in an age when apologizing and acknowledging errors or misjudgment isn’t something you see every day. If you’re really clear about it, it builds trust and helps give people one more reason to have faith in what you’re doing.

What do you hope readers take away from this project?

I hope we deepen faith in what we do. I also hope we show how we can use our archive to make history a bigger part of daily work. Newspapers are focused on today and tomorrow, and sometimes we forget yesterday. The fact is that yesterday can be a source of great journalism and useful context to help people understand the moment.

item.title: Planning a Trip With A.I.? Here’s How to Do It Better.
item.description:
If artificial intelligence can quickly find needles in legal haystacks, crack long-unsolved math problems and create retro 1980s images convincing enough to be Bon Jovi album covers, why is it so bad at planning a week in Rome?

Blame it on the prompts. Chatbots may still be a long way from replacing old-school travel planning techniques, but they can create far better results than most of us realize. The problem: We’re not helping them enough.“They’re not oracles,” said Ethan Mollick, a professor who studies A.I. and its impact at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. “Think of it like working with a smart person.”

Using advice from Dr. Mollick, other experts and tech-savvy friends, as well as tips from A.I. companies, I set out to test some theories about writing better prompts for travel planning.

I concocted two fictional five-day trips tailored to the two cities I know best: São Paulo, Brazil, and New York. I planned to prompt three bots — ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude — trying both the free and paid versions. (The paid versions tended to go deeper and work faster, and were less likely to run out of steam.)

One twist: I went undercover, using new accounts or “temporary chats” so the bots wouldn’t know that I had lived in the two cities for years. I asked A.I. to advise a first-time traveler to São Paulo and a veteran New York City visitor who had already seen all the main sights.

I was impressed by the results, if not persuaded to give up my old-fashioned predilections for tips from friends, paper guidebooks and late nights of online research.

Here are some strategies that worked for me.

Consider this typical rookie mistake: asking a bot to “plan a three-day weekend in Chicago for someone who likes museums and good food.”

Experts told me again and again, “Ask generic questions, and you’ll get generic answers.”

The results end up being bland — who doesn’t like good food? — as well as vulnerable to “generative engine optimization,” a fast-growing practice in which companies scramble to game the models so they appear in responses. (It’s the A.I. equivalent of search engine optimization, which companies have used for years to rise to the top of Google searches.)

To get more tailored results, shower the bot with personal details. That includes your specific tastes in travel, your goals for this trip and any advice you’ve already culled from friends or other sources.

Try compiling a personal travel profile with a few paragraphs about your preferences and philosophy, perhaps in a Google Doc, that you can feed into bots.

Mine included my love of “tours with very quirky local guides,” my aversion to international hotel chains and my tendency to choose restaurants based in part on online user reviews written in the language of either the destination (Paris restaurants reviewed in French) or the cuisine (Chinatown restaurants reviewed in Chinese).

Dr. Mollick urged travelers to be honest, even blunt. No chatbot will judge you if you say your ideal Chicago trip favors hot dogs over haute cuisine (and neither will most Chicagoans, as long as you lay off the ketchup).

In addition to your travel profile, you should feed the bot any other research you’ve done using your favorite sources of travel information or tips you’ve gotten from friends. The assistant will work those tips into your itinerary, or perhaps tell you why they don’t fit. For my São Paulo test, for example, I uploaded advice from a “friend I trust who lives in São Paulo.” (It was actually a document I shared with out-of-town guests who came to my wedding last year.)

A.I. can actually help you make your prompts more effective. Every step along the way, ask the bot if there is anything you can do to make your request clearer.

For example, when I uploaded my travel profile, I told each bot to ask me five follow-up questions. For the New York trip, Gemini asked about my willingness to spend several hours traveling to a more distant but interesting part of the city. I said that sounded good, but just for one day. It suggested a trip to Pelham Bay Park and City Island in the Bronx — good advice if I am the target.

ChatGPT suggested Jackson Heights, Queens, saying it “feels almost mandatory for you.” That made sense, because it also happens to be the neighborhood I lived in for more than 15 years.

For São Paulo, instead of a day-by-day agenda, I asked for four separate lists — activities, restaurants, nightlife and lodging — with “too many” choices for each one. I assumed I could pare down each list by asking the bots further questions. That worked great, and at the end I asked to group the results into geographically sensible clusters.

Unlike you and me, A.I. does not have free rein on the internet. Many websites (including The New York Times, which has sued OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and others for copyright infringement) block bots’ access to some or all of their content. Others have deals with specific A.I. companies. For example, ChatGPT and Gemini, which is owned by Google, have full access to Reddit — a great source for travel tips — while Claude, which was created by Anthropic, does not. And bots can’t necessarily see every Tripadvisor review, or the full content of many travel and food publications.

So even though bots work quickly and effectively, they have limited resources. Using one can be a bit like hiring a master chef who gets to shop only at 7-Eleven.

How do you know if a bot can search your most trusted sources of information? Name a site you like and ask the bot if it has access. For example, I am a fan of the food site Eater, which Claude and Gemini told me they could not search directly, while ChatGPT said it could. (It turns out Eater has a partnership with ChatGPT.) You can also double-check sources by asking the bot to cite the URLs it used to come up with the tips.

Sites that big-name chatbots can’t fully search sometimes offer their own A.I. bots. I tested Tripadvisor’s built-in assistant by asking it for advice about São Paulo hotels for under $150, and it did a decent job. Reddit also has a bot that allows you to mine its seemingly infinite well of travel recommendations.

Gemini trumpets its access to Google Maps information and user reviews, so I was surprised when it recommended one restaurant and one place to hear live music that were no longer open, as any human user of Maps could have figured out. “You are 100 percent correct,” the bot wrote after I called it out on the error, “and I completely deserve to be thoroughly benched on this planning session.”

My prompt also asked for lodging recommendations, asking the bots to scan user reviews and avoid any hotels with a pattern of complaints of nearby construction noise, a perennial problem in São Paulo. One of Gemini’s three choices was the Transamerica Prime International Plaza, but when I noticed it listed Expedia and Booking.com as its sources, I asked if it had also checked Google reviews. Apparently, it had not, because the bot did an about-face, responding, “Dozens of Google reviewers explicitly warn light sleepers to stay away,” noting that drilling and heavy machinery noise start early.

Claude made one blatant hallucination, recommending two traditional Brazilian bakeries “that haven’t gone gourmet.” But when I checked on Google Maps, the two places turned out to be a parking lot and a Japanese restaurant. ChatGPT didn’t make any mistakes that I caught, but that doesn’t mean there weren’t any. You should independently check every place you plan to visit.

Unless you’re never going to travel again, save your work. I found the Project feature on ChatGPT and Claude a useful way to have what amounts to a running conversation about leisure travel separate from whatever else you might be asking. It takes only a click or two to set up, and the bot can tell you how. (Gemini has no exact equivalent to Projects.)

If you create a project, you can use it during the trip to fine-tune or make a last-minute change, and even provide post-trip feedback so the bot gives you better results next time.

Think of A.I. chatbots as very smart but fallible tools that work best with long, detailed input and lots of pushback. That does not mean abandoning your time-tested travel resources, but instead using them to nourish the bot and keep it honest, or at least as honest as a virtual assistant can be.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: The High-Risk, Often Low-Paid Work of Protecting People
item.description:
Antonio Salguero pored over the checklist on his laptop: eight extra security guards, radios for guards and staff, a specific catchphrase for emergency response.

The Jewish High Holy Days, underway this week, are the busiest time of the year for Mr. Salguero, who owns a company that handles security for Congregation Beth Israel, the largest synagogue in San Diego. With thousands attending multiple special services, the logistics can get complicated.

The stakes of the work feel especially heightened these days. Threats against houses of worship, especially synagogues and mosques, are on the rise. And a few months ago, two teenagers opened fire on the Islamic Center of San Diego, the largest mosque in the region, killing three men. The shooters had also planned to attack a local synagogue.

“The risk is always there,” said Mr. Salguero. “But that shooting really hit home the reality.”

That attack resonated for people like Mr. Salguero because one of the men killed was Amin Abdullah, the security guard at the mosque’s front entrance. Mr. Abdullah ensured the mosque went into lockdown and then confronted the gunmen. He died doing his job, protecting the worshipers inside.

There are some 1.3 million people working as security guards in this country, more than the nation’s police and sheriff patrol officers, according to a report released this summer by the UC Berkeley Labor Center.

Despite their ubiquity, they are often overlooked. They wear suits or neatly pressed collared shirts. Some wear bulletproof vests and carry walkie-talkies. They keep watch outside schools and hospitals, strip malls and construction sites. Yet security guards, some of whom are unarmed, have to de-escalate mental health crises, prepare for mass casualty responses and navigate many of the same complex situations that confront law enforcement — without the same levels of training, institutional protection or pay.

The private security market is a growing $50 billion industry, but security guards earn a little less than $19 an hour — about 73 cents for every dollar earned by the typical U.S. worker, according to the Berkeley report. Most guards work for contract security firms and many don’t get health insurance through work. The work force is overwhelmingly male and around half is Black or Latino. Turnover is exceptionally high, a fact the Berkeley researchers attributed in part to low wages and poor benefits.

“They’re playing this critical public safety role, but their wages and training have not kept pace with those responsibilities and risks with the job,” said Enrique Lopezlira, a labor economist at Berkeley and an author of the report.

There is no federal training standard for security guards. Roughly half of states set a minimum number of training hours for unarmed guards, which ranges from around four to 48 hours.

The Service Employees International Union has pressed for local and state legislation to improve conditions for guards, with mixed results. In New York City, the killing of Aland Etienne, a security guard on duty during a 2025 mass shooting in Midtown Manhattan, propelled action. A law now mandates that armed guards in the city must soon make at least $33.70 an hour and unarmed guards with certain training at least $22.20. In March, Baltimore city officials implemented a similar piece of legislation.

“Security work has become one of the most dangerous occupations in America, making this more than a workplace issue,” said April Verrett, president of the S.E.I.U., in a statement. “It’s a matter of life and death.”

In California, in the wake of the San Diego mosque shooting, state lawmakers doled out $80 million in grants this spring primarily to faith based groups so they could bolster security infrastructure. But an effort to create the nation’s first statewide minimum wage for California’s estimated 330,000 private security guards faced strong pushback from the business community and was ultimately stripped of pay standards.

“Private security must remain affordable so our employees and customers are protected,” said Matthew Hargrove, president and chief executive of the California Business Properties Association.

Recently, members of the S.E.I.U.-United Service Workers West voted to authorize a strike for 14,000 security guards in Los Angeles County and the Bay Area amid contract negotiations with major security companies, such as Allied Universal and Securitas. The tension led Anthropic, which uses one of the security firms, to ask employees to work from home, according to reports.

Gerald Walker, 65, has patrolled the lobby of a downtown San Diego office building for 12 years. He spends his shifts scrutinizing the cameras and the people who come and go.

He enjoys the work, especially catching up with regulars in the building, but when he arrives each morning for his shift at 7 he knows he faces some risk. He has had some tense moments. A man once flashed a knife at him. Another time, he was punched in the face by someone as he held open a door.

“We are the first responders,” said Mr. Walker, who is a member of the S.E.I.U.

He has had only limited training in de-escalation through his employer, so he often uses common sense. Not infrequently he calls the police for help. Mr. Walker, who is unarmed, earns $21 an hour — not enough, he said, to keep up with inflation and the increasingly high costs of living in Southern California. He has a side gig as a personal trainer to make ends meet.

For Mr. Walker and many other security guards in Southern California, the death of Mr. Abdullah, the guard at the Islamic Center, was a tragedy that reinforced the risks of their job.

Taha Hassane, the center’s imam, was the last person to speak with Mr. Abdullah at his post inside the guard shack on May 18.

About 10 minutes later, Mr. Abdullah radioed to initiate the mosque’s emergency lockdown protocol and exchanged fire with the shooters, actions that the authorities say saved the lives of dozens of children and congregants gathered inside. Mr. Abdullah was an independent contractor, who worked shifts at the center where he was also a member.

Mr. Hassane said the mosque had armed security for the last decade.

“We want this to be a welcoming place,” he said. “But it’s the world we live in.”

Rabbi Cantor Jeremy Gimbel of Congregation Beth Israel agrees. “We have it because we need it,” he said of the security team, adding that congregants “breathe easier” when they see armed guards at the entrance.

Mr. Salguero was at home when the mosque shooting occurred.

He heard about it through his regular communication with a coalition of local security companies, and by the time he reached out to colleagues on duty that day the synagogue was already on lockdown.

Members of the congregation had felt on edge since a 2019 mass shooting at a synagogue in suburban San Diego. Those fears only grew with the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, after which the congregation received emailed bomb threats, according to Mr. Salguero.

During a separate incident, he said, a driver of an S.U.V. drove past the front of the synagogue and started spewing antisemitic hate. Since the Oct. 7 attacks, he said, the security team always keeps one of the front gates locked.

“Now we just have one way in and one way out of the parking lot,” Mr. Salguero said on a recent afternoon. Children giggled with laughter from a nearby courtyard. Gates guarding the synagogue clanged open and closed as people came and went.

item.title: Why the Fed Might Raise Rates When Borrowing Costs Are Surging
item.description:
Since the start of the year, Americans have been paying more to secure mortgages and auto loans, as well as to pay down their credit card debts.

And as higher prices are also burning a larger hole in consumers’ wallets, it may seem counterintuitive that the Federal Reserve is expected to make borrowing costs even higher by raising rates on Wednesday.

.

But the reason stems from the fact that even though rates are higher than they were for much of the first two decades of the 2000s, consumer spending, business investment and other measures of the health of the economy are all running hot. And inflation, the rise in prices that can result from such vigorous spending, has hovered above the Fed’s 2 percent target rate for half a decade.

“Raising interest rates is specifically intended to deter spending,” said Thierry Wizman, a strategist on global fixed income and rates at investment bank Macquarie Group. “So the pain that the consumer is feeling if they’re obligated to pay more on a home, or a car loan, or on a student loan, is intentional.”

In 2022, before the Fed began a period of inflation-induced increases, interest rates hovered around zero. They rose to between 5.25 percent and 5.5 percent in 2023. Today, they sit between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent.

These rates determine short-term borrowing costs. When they go up, lending conditions for banks tighten, creating a domino effect that can reduce consumer spending and business investment. But so far, higher rates have not done much to slow the economy.

Americans spent $36 billion more in the U.S. economy in July compared with the month before, according to the latest personal expenditures report from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The boost in spending was driven by a robust labor market that has pumped up wages and Americans’ disposable income.

For a while, this spending has been uneven across income brackets in the United States. This is what has been described as the “K-shaped” economy, with the less wealthy represented by the lower-trending line and the wealthy the upward-trending line.

“Not everyone owns a home and not everyone owns equities — but it’s that part of the economy, the consumer, that’s been driving growth, the upper part of that ‘K,’” said Leslie Falconio, head of fixed income strategy for UBS Global Wealth Management.

Still, there are signs of convergence in that lopsided picture, according to analysts who examined credit card spending data from Bank of America. Spending by lower income consumers has risen disproportionately in recent months, they said.

Business investment is also booming, propelled by investors’ betting that returns from artificial intelligence will outpace the cost of borrowing. The stock market is reflecting confidence in tech as well, bolstered by a blockbuster earnings season. The S&P 500 is up roughly 11 percent since the start of the year.

Part of the Fed’s mandate is to maintain stable prices. Inflation is still ringing in at more than 2 percent year-over-year — where the Fed would like it — with the numbers for August coming in hotter than expected. A big driver of inflation has been an energy crunch set off by the disruption of global oil flows in the Middle East. The global price of oil has risen 15 percent this month alone.

Perhaps the only sector that has relented in the face of higher rates is the housing market. Home sales are falling as mortgage rates have crossed 6.7 percent for the first time since July 2025. But many homeowners able to lock in mortgages at lower rates secured years ago have been able to reduce the strain on their wallets.

“That resiliency and that growth outlook that continues to be strong allows the Fed to say, ‘OK, I’m going to continue to focus on this price-stability side, because the interest rates aren’t restrictive and we can hike — growth isn’t teetering,’” Ms. Falconio said.

The Fed’s policy path most directly affects interest rates, or yields, on shorter-term U.S. Treasuries, like the two-year note. Longer-term yields move based on Fed policy but give more weight to factors like inflation and the national deficit.

The two-year bill has ticked up to 4.66 percent for the first time since 2024. The 10-year note, which sets the pace for most consumer loans, has punched past 5 percent this week, the highest level since 2023.

Markets have priced in a rate increase at the Fed’s meeting on Wednesday so a hike this week would help those yields ease lower, Ms. Falconio said.

It would signal to investors that the board is proactive about managing inflation, coaxing them to expect inflation to moderate and demand a lower return on long-term government bonds, she said.

That easing would take time to translate into lower rates for consumers.

“If growth stays resilient, and they hike five or six times, then the long end is not going to go down,” Ms. Falconio said about long-term bonds. “It really depends on how many times they hike.”

item.title: Fed Readies for Momentous Rate Decision
item.description:
The Federal Reserve is on the cusp of a momentous decision on Wednesday. The central bank is widely expected to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to a new range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent.

If the Fed follows through, it will be the first rate increase since July 2023. It would also immediately put Kevin M. Warsh, who took over as chairman in May, in the cross hairs of President Trump less than two months before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress.

Just days before the Fed’s September gathering, Mr. Trump reiterated that the United States “should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world.” That followed the president’s threat this month that he would cut off a broad swath of U.S. trade if the Fed did not lower rates.

On Wednesday, the Fed will release its rate decision at 2 p.m. in Washington. Mr. Warsh will hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m.

Here is what to watch for:

The number of dissents will depend on what decision the Fed makes. Holding rates steady would generate at minimum three opposing votes, probably from the same officials who voted against the Fed’s decision to do exactly that in July.

Back then, Beth M. Hammack of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of the Minneapolis Fed and Lorie K. Logan of the Dallas Fed voted in favor of a quarter-point increase. They argued that higher rates would have put the central bank in a better position to tackle elevated inflation.

Many officials have since sent a consistent message that if inflation does not soon ease, they will be prepared to raise rates. Financial markets overwhelmingly believe that this condition has been met, with the odds of a rate increase now above 90 percent. As a result, Mr. Warsh and his colleagues on the policy-making committee have limited latitude to avoid lifting rates.

One of the most effective ways for the Fed to send a clear message on Wednesday that it is serious about tackling inflation is for there to be zero dissents to raising rates. That is not guaranteed, however.

Several top officials sought to carve out flexibility for the Fed ahead of September’s gathering. They included both John C. Williams, who as president of the New York Fed is the vice-chair of the Federal Open Market Committee, and Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor. Neither conveyed an urgency to raise rates, but each indicated that hotter inflation data would clinch the case to proceed.

August’s inflation data, which came in higher than expected, probably met that threshold, suggesting both will support a decision to raise rates if Mr. Warsh pushes the committee in that direction.

Perhaps as important as the move itself is the rationalization that Mr. Warsh provides for proceeding with a rate increase. How he frames the decision will heavily influence expectations for what the Fed does next.

Rate moves are rarely one-offs, meaning it is more likely that the central bank will deliver a series of increases. The question is not only how many there are but also how far apart they will be spaced.

Most economists see the Fed raising rates again in December. The next meeting is in October, just days before the midterms, so unless inflation has taken a material turn for the worse, the central bank could easily hold off on taking action to avoid the perception that it is having any impact on the outcome.

Additional adjustments are on the table for 2027, but Mr. Warsh is unlikely to be specific about his plans.

That is partly a function of how uncertain the economic backdrop has become. Inflation is forecast to decelerate as the year progresses, but the pace is unclear, especially with the Iran war dragging on. At the same time, Mr. Warsh has purposely sought to keep things vague in order to retain flexibility for the Fed.

His predecessors would probably have leaned on the so-called dot plot, set to be updated on Wednesday, that tracks how officials see the trajectory for rates, growth, unemployment and inflation in the years to come. It is expected to show additional rate increases this year and next, helping to bound expectations about what the Fed has in store for borrowing costs.

However, Mr. Warsh is an avowed critic of the dot plot and has opted against submitting his own projections. If he dismisses the dot plot altogether, that could create confusion over how aggressively the Fed is prepared to act.

Mr. Warsh was swiftly rebuked by markets after his last meeting in July, when he sent mixed signals about the Fed’s commitment to reducing inflation back to 2 percent. Longer-term U.S. borrowing costs shot higher as investors pushed back the timing of potential rate increases until later this year.

Holding rates steady in September would risk a redux of that, especially after Mr. Warsh sent such a strong signal at his latest public appearance last month that he was indeed serious about his inflation pledge.

That kind of reaction would prove problematic for the Trump administration, which has taken aggressive steps over the past month to contain longer-dated borrowing costs. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has intervened in the bond market in a variety of ways, including most recently by buying back bonds outright. That has done little to quell Treasury yields. The 10-year Treasury yield, one of the most important interest rates in the world, is now trading around 5 percent, the highest level in years.

While the Trump administration is clear in its desire for lower rates from the central bank, a Fed that demonstrates its resolve in getting inflation down could help to keep overall borrowing costs set by market forces lower than would otherwise be the case.

With affordability issues top of mind ahead of the midterms, that outcome would be advantageous for the White House, investors say.

item.title: A ‘Shark’ of a Business Editor Steps Down
item.description:
When Ellen Pollock, the longtime Business editor of The New York Times, calls in to a video meeting, she’s often in front of a virtual background resembling the deck of a spaceship. It’s a whimsical touch with a serious message: She is at the controls.

After nearly a decade atop one of the largest news desks at The Times, Pollock has decided to leave the role this month. She took over the desk in 2017 after stints as a reporter and an editor at The American Lawyer, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg Businessweek, where she was editor in chief.

She hasn’t announced what she’ll do next in The Times’s newsroom, only that she intends to take a break first. We used this occasion to talk about her tenure, the business world and the challenges facing journalism. These are edited excerpts from our conversation.

Nine years is a long run as a department head at The Times. These are stressful management roles with responsibility for overseeing competitive coverage and a large staff. How did you endure?

Momentum and instinct help a lot. Nobody gets into this kind of work without being aggressive and wanting to win — so that has helped keep me going. If I were a fish, and for the record I’m glad I’m not, I’d definitely be a shark.

But the main thing that motivates anyone in my kind of job is the desire to inform readers and get them the truth — as soon as possible and with as much explanation and nuance as possible. It’s a mission. And even if that sounds kind of corny, it’s true.

Every morning I walk through the front door, past the historic front pages displayed in the lobby, and remind myself how lucky I am — even on days when I’m very grumpy.

What was the toughest story or leadership challenge you faced?

I’m not sure what was the toughest, but certainly Covid was a very difficult time. From a coverage standpoint, it was a monster. We started out covering mask, ventilator and hand sanitizer shortages and quickly moved on to plunging stock markets and job losses suffered by millions of Americans. The government swooped in with benefits, but those benefits would expire. It seemed like the economy — and the finances of our readers — were constantly on the verge of falling off a cliff. Seems like we used the word cliff a lot.

Our job was to guide readers through it all and explain the possible scenarios without predicting the future, because nobody could do that. I think our reporters and editors really rose to the occasion.

At the same time, our staff was scattered to the winds. Just keeping track of how everybody was doing was impossible. We hired people during that period who didn’t know their colleagues or anything about working at The Times.

I spent the first week after the lockdown sitting on the floor of my apartment hunched over my computer, and when I finally stood up I realized my back had gone out. I could barely walk for months and, like millions of other people, I learned how hard it was to get medical help and how brave the medical personnel were during the pandemic.

I was glad to return to the newsroom.

You’ve run coverage, but you’ve also navigated the bureaucratic nature of a large company. Have you ever disagreed with your bosses on a story or approach?

When it comes to our approach to coverage, and what’s important, we almost always agree. We sometimes disagree on priorities, what is realistic and timing. I’m fine with discussing and debating. I think that often yields better and more thoughtful results.

Sometimes figuring out how to follow up on breaking news can be tricky. We jump on the news. But then do we quickly push out a follow-up story? Or do we take an extra day to produce something more in-depth and explanatory? There’s sometimes some tension there.

And I’m grouchy about some meetings and the increasing number of administrative tasks that happen at a growing organization. In general, I’m not fond of the Three Bs: bureaucracy, bullshit and boredom.

You are known as a truth-teller who is unafraid to speak your mind to colleagues and bosses alike, including a sprinkle of salty language. Has it ever backfired?

Backfired! It’s a miracle I still have a job! A year or so ago, I threatened to kill a reporter if his story ended up too long. That was bad — and certainly an overreaction. The “news” got picked up in the press. (I promise you, I’m armed with chocolate not weapons.) Another time I told a boss that she had disrespected me. That didn’t go over so well, either. One thing I haven’t learned yet is to keep my mouth shut. But I have learned to apologize. Next I’m going to tackle groveling.

Some business leaders and readers see Times business coverage as adversarial to companies, C.E.O.s, capitalism, Big Tech and A.I. You’re tough-nosed about coverage, but do you see it as hostile?

I absolutely don’t see it as hostile, and the idea that we have something against companies or A.I. or chief executives really frustrates me — I’m trying to avoid salty language here. We cover business the way we cover anything else. We want to break news, convey the truth without bias and reveal what happens behind the scenes so that readers can understand how money and power work. We are interested in companies and the people who run companies and make policy. We want our readers to understand markets and how their money is invested. If you have a 401(k) or pension, you’re a shareholder. We want you to know how your companies work. Readers are interested in who makes the ice cream they slurp and the computers they pound on. We are here to inform and, when necessary, reveal secrets. That’s it.

I find the view that we are against capitalism to be particularly galling. I love money and want more of it!

Part of your jurisdiction is the media beat — reporting on the journalism industry and the powers and people who shape it. Sometimes that means covering The Times. How does that work?

We try to cover The Times the way we cover any other company, but obviously a host of questions come up that can be a little delicate. Just like covering anything else, sometimes we don’t get all the answers we want, when we want them. Then we have to go digging. That can get a little awkward, but usually it is pretty smooth.

More than once I’ve glared at senior people at The Times and said, “We don’t want to get beat on this story.” That sometimes works.

The Times has been involved in a fair amount of litigation that involves press freedom and copyright. We have been sued by President Trump. All those issues can be complicated, and we need to cover them dispassionately and with independence. So we are constantly checking ourselves and one another.

There’s a tiny bit of fun stuff sprinkled in. In 2022, when the company bought Wordle, the word game, more than one department wanted to write the story. The Business department won out!

You are known in the newsroom for your career advice to women who are early in their careers. Did someone do the same for you?

Not really. I never had an early career mentor. But I had a lot of co-workers who were women, and we all supported one another and made one another laugh. Early on I had an editor, Denise Martin, who taught me the basic skills of writing, and I am forever grateful to her. And many years later I had a boss, Carol Hymowitz, who had arrived at The Wall Street Journal when there were fewer women at the paper. She was incredibly supportive.

During the early years of my career, there was plenty of ugliness. There was harassment. Women weren’t taken seriously and were just plain looked down upon. There was a lot of disparaging language that you don’t hear much today. You kind of had to blast through it, but it was pretty wearing.

And of course men still strut around like they rule the world. So the story isn’t over yet.

You’ve talked about the never-ending news cycle, about interrupted and missed dinners with family and friends. What kind of toll has the job taken on you?

So many times I have raced out of restaurants in the middle of a meal with friends to take a call about news. Inevitably it is either 16 degrees or 98 degrees on the sidewalk. There’s also nothing like dragging a laptop to a dinner party. Hosts love it when you set up an office in their kitchen while everyone else is in the dining room.

There are a lot of novels I haven’t read. I have friends I haven’t kept up with. I’m a lousy friend, and I feel awful about it.

Your daughter has followed in your footsteps. What do you make of her decision to pursue journalism despite all the threats to the industry?

My husband, who retired from The Times, tried to steer my daughter away from being a reporter, but she refused to listen!

My daughter is pretty young and has a good gig in journalism, so I’m very proud of her. When I see her byline, I totally turn 100 percent mom and get so excited. As a mom and editor, I worry endlessly about the news business, which seems beset by one existential threat after another. So I’m keeping my fingers crossed for her and journalism that readers stick with us and that the demand for independent news gathering goes up and not down.

What are you watching for next in the business world?

I’ve stopped predicting what’s going to happen. The economist Paul Samuelson once said something to the effect that Wall Street indexes had predicted nine out of the previous five recessions. I’ll just go out on a limb here to say that in the next year markets will either go up or down. Unless they stay flat.

item.title: Fed Meeting Will Test Central Bank’s Credibility With Bond Investors
item.description:
Investors expect that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates on Wednesday in a bid to curb inflation, with bets in financial markets pointing to a 90 percent likelihood of a quarter-point increase.

But bond investors are still on edge, mindful of a new, less predictable leader of the central bank in Kevin M. Warsh. If the Fed doesn’t lift rates, then investors will probably question the central bank’s commitment to containing inflation, prompting them to increase their own forecasts for price pressure and injecting new turmoil into the government bond market.

Already, the 30-year Treasury yield is at its highest level in nearly two decades and the 10-year yield is flirting with a similar milestone. These yields provide the bedrock of the global financial system, used as a benchmark to establish borrowing costs for companies seeking loans and consumers taking out mortgages.

“If the Fed has credibility on policy then you see inflation expectations remain contained,” said Subadra Rajappa, an interest rate strategist at Societe Generale. “If they don’t respond to inflation, and when they can’t control inflation, that is when you are going to start to see more wild price action.”

Inflation pressure has been building as a result of America’s attack on Iran at the end of February and the sharp rise in oil prices that resulted. But until recently, that inflation pressure has mostly remained a short-term worry, one that bond investors believe can be solved over the next few years, precisely because they expect the Fed to act.

Investors with a longer-term view have instead focused their worries on tariffs, tax cuts, government spending and, especially, on the soaring spending (and borrowing) from artificial intelligence companies. The expectation that higher inflation persists for the next 10 or even 30 years has not been a major concern, based on market prices.

The 10-year break-even inflation rate, a market measure of investors’ inflation expectations over the next decade, stands at around 2.4 percent, modestly above the Fed’s long-term target of 2 percent. That measure fell to a low for the year of 2.2 percent in June, when the war with Iran appeared to be winding down.

“If they don’t hike, the risk is that inflation expectations, particularly at the long end, start to rise,” said Brendan Murphy, head of fixed income for North America at Insight Investment.

And there is the potential for a longer lasting impact for Fed officials when it comes to fighting inflation. “The market starts to think they are not credible,” he added.

The tension around Wednesday’s meeting reflects a sharp shift in expectations under President Trump, who has repeatedly said he wants to see interest rates move lower, handpicking Mr. Warsh to do just that.

The day before Donald Trump attacked Iran at the end of February, investors expected the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point twice through the end of the year. Now they expect the central bank to raise them as many as four times through next year.

When Mr. Warsh took helm of the Fed in May, he committed to a new communication style that limited guidance for investors about what the Fed might do next. As part of this approach, Mr. Warsh initially refused to commit to lifting interest rates in response to growing inflation pressure, amping angst among bond investors left unsure of how the central bank would now respond to rising inflation.

Then in August, investors interpreted a speech by Mr. Warsh to be a signal that if inflation pressures remained, he would raise interest rates. Data released this month showed prices throughout the economy continued to rise in August, and investors are now looking for Mr. Warsh to make good on his perceived commitment.

George Goncalves, an interest rate strategist at MUFG Americas, worries that interest rates have already moved too far, too quickly, and that the result could slow the economy more in the coming months than is currently expected. Still, he expects the Fed to elevate interest rates to maintain its credibility.

“You have to now hike,” he said. “You can’t really not hike.”

item.title: Toronto Film Festival Mixes Business With Moviegoing Pleasure
item.description:
The booths, lounges and displays fill the third-floor exhibition hall of the Metro Toronto Convention Center.

Some are manned by representatives of film commissions from around the world, promoting their countries as shooting locations, or hawking local projects in handouts, postcards and branded knickknacks. Production companies, seeking foreign distribution for completed films or potential ones, display posters and play trailers. The booth for RDV Canada, an initiative to promote the local film industry, is the busiest at the moment, the site of a reception, with finger food and beverages aplenty.

Most important, everywhere you look there are tables ready for distributors, executives, agents and filmmakers to pull up a chair and make a deal.

This giant hall is the centerpiece of TIFF: The Market, the newest addition to the long-running Toronto International Film Festival. It is, at least on the surface, a striking departure from the event’s hard-earned reputation. “TIFF was — or is — a festival festival,” Anna Godas, chief executive of the documentary distribution company Dogwoof, said in an interview. “You go to watch films, and the perception, at least for us, is that buyers go there to watch films and not necessarily to do a bunch of meetings.”

But the festival has been contemplating expansion for quite some time. According to its chief executive, Cameron Bailey, the organization began looking into the possibility of adding a market component as early as 2012 — moving from its long-held position as an exhibition-only event, like the New York Film Festival, to a hybrid along the lines of Cannes or Berlin. At those events, the glamorous screenings, red carpets and news conferences exist side by side with a busy market, where film packages are presented, pitches are made and deals are closed.

“The research said there would be an opportunity,” Bailey explained in an interview. “There wasn’t anything similar in North America to what existed in Europe.” TIFF wasn’t yet ready to take that leap, but the idea continued to percolate, and in 2024, the organization announced — with the backing of the Canadian federal government, to the tune of $23 million — the addition of an official market alongside the festival, beginning this year.

For TIFF, it’s also a financial opportunity — a necessary one. Following the pandemic, TIFF weathered staff cuts, sponsorship losses and other economic challenges. The Market offers several revenue possibilities, from increased attendance for buyers and sellers and booth rentals on the exhibition floor. But Bailey emphasized that the addition represents a long-term advantage: “It’s not something that immediately is going to change the financial picture for the organization.”

John Sloss, a sales agent and producer who has attended the festival for at least 35 years, noted in a phone interview that “TIFF has been a de facto market forever, because it’s such a huge festival and it’s such a critical launchpad for all the releases, and all the buyers and sellers are there. The idea of creating a more formalized structure for it strikes me as a good idea.”

That view was shared by Charles Tremblay, a longtime distributor and film executive who joined the festival to head up the Market. “My general reaction was, ‘What took you so long?’” he recalled in an interview. “I always felt that there could be more — there was maybe a bit of a missed opportunity.”

Much of the industry has shared his enthusiasm. But some observers worried that such an explicitly business-oriented approach was contrary to the festival’s ethos. In a 1991 interview with Roger Ebert, a TIFF co-founder, Dusty Cohl, explained what distinguished the Toronto event from, say, Cannes: “This one is designed for the people who come and watch films, people who love films.”

So is TIFF betraying the spirit in which it was founded? Bailey doesn’t think so. “It’s a long way from 1991 to 2026,” he said. “It was an entirely different ecosystem, and we didn’t have to question it or worry about whether it would always be there. It’s very different now, so the Market will help us to sustain the kind of films that we love and want to see more of.”

The producer and director Robert Vince said he was surprised it took so long to formalize a structure “because it really has been a quasi-marketplace,” he said in an interview. Vince should know; his 1997 comedy “Air Bud” was sold to Disney out of TIFF, and now, nearly 30 years and 14 films later, he’s at the Market to sell the series’s latest installment, “Air Bud Returns.”

“It’s kind of a big moment,” he said with a grin. “We’re back to our independent roots.”

In the meantime, the Market can be seen as an attempt “to regain some momentum following Covid, which arguably affected Toronto more than other festivals,” Sloss said. “I think the Market is sort of a statement, that they want to reinforce their prominence as the granddaddy of fall festivals, or at least comparable events.”

And as a bonus, its centralized location can attract more filmmakers. “We thought about going to Cannes, but we’re working-class filmmakers,” said the producer John Flynn, manning a booth for the independent film “Binary Star.” “We can’t afford to go to every single major event, especially overseas.”

Many foreign buyers don’t go to Toronto, said Marc Goldberg, founder of the production and distribution company Signature Entertainment, explaining in an interview that “it’s only ever been a festival.”

Some may be hesitant to add it to their calendar, with the long-running American Film Market in Los Angeles just two months later. But some overseas buyers may be reluctant, in the current political climate, to travel to the United States, making Toronto a sensible alternative.

The integration of the Market hasn’t been all smooth sailing. Some attendees were stymied by long lines at registration — “We got here at 7 a.m.,” Flynn said, “and then by 7:45, the line was almost out of the building” — and some exhibitors reported slower foot traffic than they’d hoped, primarily because of the floor’s geographical separation several blocks from the screening sites.

Shreyans Hirawat, director of the India-based NH Studioz, reported few brand-new contacts on the Market floor. “But even the few who were there had good, quality time to spend,” he added. “Unlike other film festivals, where you’re in a rush, here people had that time.”

These are growing pains, Bailey hopes. “I think the Market is going to be a big part of bringing people together,” he said. “It’s happened informally in really beautiful ways in the past,” he added, recalling the time Chloé Zhao brought “The Rider” to the festival the same year that Frances McDormand was attending. “They met and they actually decided to work on ‘Nomadland’ together here in Toronto.”

“So if you have not just the festival facilitating that, but a market facilitating that as well,” Bailey said, “I think what we get is Toronto being a real, essential hub for the art and business of film.”

item.title: Saudi Pipeline Attack Risks ‘Disastrous’ Loss of Millions of Barrels of Oil
item.description:
The continued closure of a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia risks keeping 4 percent of the world’s oil supply from reaching international markets and driving energy prices even higher.

Saudi Arabia scrambled this week to reroute roughly four million barrels of oil a day when it temporarily shut its East-West pipeline, which it said on Friday was damaged by an Iran-backed militia. The pipeline, a 750-mile network that transports crude across Saudi Arabia to ports on the Red Sea, had been the kingdom’s primary way of exporting oil since the war in Iran began in February.

And there are scant signs that the threat to Saudi oil supplies will ease anytime soon. In addition to the drone attack on the pipeline, the Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group in Yemen gained control of a strategic Red Sea port and hit energy facilities in Saudi Arabia. On Wednesday the Houthis claimed they had downed a Saudi fighter jet, as Saudi Arabia said the Houthis had fired a drone near the Muslim holy city of Mecca.

Now, running out of options and under pressure to rapidly restore supply lines, Saudi Arabia is facing the prospect of a severe energy crisis with global implications, analysts said.

“It is unprecedented,” said Amena Bakr, head of Middle East & OPEC+ Insights at Kpler, a maritime data firm.

“We have two major waterways obstructed, active attacks, Iran escalating attacks, proxies being active and no signs of diplomatic talks,” Ms. Bakr said. “It’s a disastrous situation when you’re looking at it from an energy security angle.”

Any extended disruption to the pipeline network of Saudi Arabia, long the world’s biggest oil exporter, would send shock waves through the global energy market. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, hovered around $107 per barrel on Wednesday, up 50 percent from its prewar level.

The world could lose 120 million barrels of crude if the East-West Pipeline is offline for a month, according to estimates from Kpler.

Goldman Sachs warned that global oil prices could rise as high as $120 a barrel if attacks in the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea continue.

The precise amount of oil not making it to the global market will depend largely on the severity of the damage to the East-West pipeline. Neither the Saudi government nor Saudi Aramco, the national oil company, responded to requests for comment.

Saudi officials previously said only that the pipeline was shut as a precaution but have not disclosed the extent of the damage or a timetable for how long it might take to restart it. Satellite images taken on Sept. 10 and 11, reviewed by The New York Times, show damage at two pumping stations on the pipeline.

Estimates for how long it might take to get the pipeline running again vary widely.

Ms. Bakr, the Kpler analyst, said she believed it could take five to six weeks, but that partial repairs could be completed far sooner.

She and others noted that the kingdom has extensive experience dealing with attacks on infrastructure. In 2019, Aramco suffered a major Houthi attack on its facilities and was able to restart pumping operations within a few days. And in April, when a pumping station was attacked shortly after the war in Iran began, full capacity was restored within seven days.

Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank, said he did not believe the “nightmare scenarios” that the pipeline could be offline for months.

“This attack has again raised in markets the fear that we could be on the cusp of another big spike,” Mr. Brooks said. But, he said, “The track record is that these things get repaired within weeks, and there’s already indications from satellite imagery that repairs are happening.”

Chris Wright, the U.S. energy secretary, said he believed oil flows through the pipeline would resume soon. “This will be a brief and temporary interruption,” Mr. Wright told CNBC on Tuesday.

Saudi Arabia has oil stored across the country, including the capacity for about 24 million barrels at its Red Sea port at Yanbu, creating a cushion. But those storage tanks are unlikely to be full, according to Rystad Energy, a consulting firm that estimated the port has about three to six days’ worth of crude.

The East-West pipeline was Saudi Arabia’s workaround when the war in Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz. Stretching from Abqaiq in the east to the Red Sea oil terminal of Yanbu in the west, the pipeline bypasses the strait entirely. Oil could be transported through the Bab al-Mandab Strait on the southern end of the Red Sea or via the Suez Canal and a pipeline across Egypt at the northern end of the sea, headed primarily to customers in Asia.

Yasir O. Al-Rumayyan, the chairman of Aramco, said in June that engineers had expanded the pipeline’s capacity to carry up to seven million barrels per day, nearly 30 percent more than before the war.

“We had a similar situation back in the ’80s, where the Strait of Hormuz was threatened to be blockaded by the Iranian regime,” Mr. Al-Rumayyan said. “It was decided since then that we will have a pipeline from east to west.”

With the Houthis now largely in control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Saudi Arabia is once again steering vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, analysts said. Since Sept. 7, just two Saudi vessels have traveled through the Red Sea, according to Kpler.

The U.S. Navy has been able to keep some oil flowing out of the Strait of Hormuz on sea paths close to the coast of Oman, the opposite side from Iran. But those efforts have required an extensive and dangerous operation.

Capital Economics, an economic research firm, said that every week the East-West pipeline is closed, while the Strait of Hormuz is off limits, will shave at least 0.2 percent off Saudi Arabia’s economic activity.

item.title: In Silicon Valley, Hardware Is Having a Moment Again
item.description:
After ChatGPT debuted in 2022, the venture capital industry raced to invest in artificial intelligence start-ups. Most V.C.s were hoping to piggyback off the success of OpenAI’s transformational chatbot. But Wen Hsieh saw the opportunity a little differently.

A hardware investor for most of his career, Mr. Hsieh recognized that an A.I. boom would create demand for the technology to power it. In 2023, he started Matter Venture Partners to focus on that bet.

It was a prescient move: Hardware is now Silicon Valley’s new buzzword.

A growing number of investors are putting their money into physical technology as A.I. disrupts venture capital’s bread-and-butter: software. In 2020, venture capital firms invested $23 billion in so-called deep tech, a category which includes robotics, space, quantum and other hardware technologies. So far this year that number has grown to $90 billion, according to Pitchbook.

“I couldn’t have imagined the day” when so many investors would become interested in hardware, Mr. Hsieh said.

That interest has served him well: Today, Matter is announcing that it has raised $450 million for its second venture fund to invest in early stage hard-tech companies. The fund-raising round includes a range of investors closely tied to the A.I. boom, including ASML, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Kleiner Perkins, where Mr. Hsieh was a general partner and worked for 17 years before cofounding Matter.

Matter invests in six core categories: semiconductors, A.I. infrastructure, energy, robotics, advanced manufacturing and quantum computing. Those industries have been viewed with caution by much of the venture industry because of the high upfront investment required to develop and build new physical products.

But A.I. has begun to change that calculation. Using A.I. models has lowered the cost and time of research and development. It has also made cheaper-to-build software products less defensible, a concern that triggered a sell-off in “software-as-a-service” stocks earlier this year in the so-called “SaaSpocalypse.”

Silicon Valley’s embrace of physical technology is perhaps best exemplified by the venture capital behemoth Andreessen Horowitz. The firm’s success was built on a philosophy — penned in a 2011 essay by its co-founder Marc Andreessen — that software is eating the world. But Andreessen Horowitz is growing its focus on physical tech too, illustrated by the $1.1 billion Machine Age fund it raised last month to invest in A.I infrastructure start-ups.

Another factor supporting hardware start-ups is the growing success of much larger hardware companies. “You’ve seen some of the most valuable businesses in the world end up being capital-intensive businesses, like SpaceX,” said Ian Samuels, the founder of the venture capital firm New System Ventures.

Investing in other hard tech start-ups “is a way to contribute to the A.I. ecosystem” and learn about innovation in the field, Arnab Das, the chief strategy officer at ASML, told DealBook.

ASML is an investor in Matter’s latest fund and is planning to establish a formal venture capital arm to invest in more start-ups. The Netherlands-based manufacturing company supplies critical parts to the semiconductor industry.

Larger companies are also showing a willingness to “pay a handsome sum” for small hardware start-ups, Mr. Hsieh said. Matter’s portfolio company Q.ai, for example, was acquired by Apple in January in a deal valued at $1.6 billion.

This is not the first time venture investors have pivoted to hardware. In the 2000s, venture capital dollars poured into clean technology companies, many of which sputtered out. And in 2020 and 2021, a public market wave of SPACs, or special purpose acquisition companies, and high-profile initial public offerings helped bring in capital for hard-tech companies, many of which have fallen in value.

The challenge and complexity of hardware investing is why investors with technical backgrounds and a long-term focus on the category are best positioned, Mr. Hsieh said: “If you’ve been doing it long enough, you know that it’s not easy to do.”
